figures.caption: LEANN System Diagram. The system combines high-degree preserving graph pruning for minimal storage footprint with graph-based recomputation and two-level search with dynamic batching for efficient query processing (Steps 1-4).

citing_sentences: Figure 1 shows the end-to-end workflow of LEANN, which includes offline index construction and online query serving.

figures.caption: Storage consumption of different vector index methods on the RPJ-Wiki dataset. The black dashed line marks the raw dataset size (76 GB), while the red dashed line shows the typical RAM capacity (32 GB, RTX 4090, following our testbed configuration in Section 7.1). Memory-heavy methods like HNSW exceed this RAM limit and cannot run on such hardware. LEANN achieves the lowest storage footprint at only 5% of the original dataset size.
figures.headline: LEANN and IVF-Recompute stay under 5% of the 76 GB raw dataset, while HNSW exceeds the 32 GB RAM limit.
citing_sentences: We compare the storage consumption of all baselines and LEANN in Figure 3.
Among all baselines, only BM25, PQ, IVF-Recompute, and LEANN maintain storage overhead below the size of the raw dataset, as shown in Figure 3.

figures.caption: Comparison of Exact Match and F1 scores for downstream RAG tasks across four methods: keyword search (BM25), PQ-compressed vector search, HNSW, and LEANN. HNSW and LEANN are configured to achieve a target recall of 90%, while the PQ baseline is given extended search time to reach its highest possible recall. Here we use Qwen3-4B as the generation model.
figures.headline: LEANN scores above BM25 and PQ on all four QA datasets and matches HNSW accuracy at 90% recall.

To evaluate RAG accuracy, we compare all retrieval methods on four QA datasets using Exact Match (EM) and F1 as metrics, as shown in Figure 4.
As shown in Figure 4, LEANN consistently outperforms BM25 and PQ across all datasets.

The dashed gray line represents the original HNSW graph as a baseline reference, which uses twice the storage (i.e., average degree) of the pruned methods.

We evaluate graph quality by measuring the number of nodes that must be recomputed to achieve a given recall target, as shown in Figure 6.
As shown in Figure 6, our pruning method introduced in Section 5 achieves performance comparable to the original unpruned graph, while using only half the edges.

abstract: Embedding-based vector search underpins many important applications, such as recommendation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It relies on vector indices to enable efficient search. However, these indices require storing high-dimensional embeddings and large index metadata, whose total size can be several times larger than the original data (e.g., text chunks). Such high storage overhead makes it difficult, or even impractical, to deploy vector search on personal devices or large-scale datasets. To tackle this problem, we propose LEANN, a storage-efficient index for vector search that recomputes embeddings on the fly instead of storing them, and compresses state-of-the-art proximity graph indices while preserving search accuracy. LEANN delivers high-quality vector search while using only a fraction of the storage (e.g., 5% of the original data) and supporting storage-efficient index construction and updates. On real-world benchmarks, LEANN reduces index size by up to 50$\times$ compared with conventional indices, while maintaining SOTA accuracy and comparable latency for RAG applications.

sections.body: Table 1 uses a 76 GB text datastore, Qwen3-4B, and an RTX 4090. HNSW needs 188 GB and BM25 needs 59 GB, while PQ needs 20 GB and LEANN needs 4 GB. Downstream accuracy is 25.5 for HNSW and LEANN, 18.3 for BM25, and 17.9 for PQ. Response generation takes over 20 s, so search latency matters less: LEANN end-to-end latency is 23.34 s against 20.95 s for HNSW, with search at 2.48 s versus 0.05 s. The section states that PQ at a high compression ratio falls below BM25 accuracy, and that the 15 GB HNSW metadata cannot be reduced by vector quantization. LEANN therefore recomputes embeddings at query time and prunes graph edges.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Graph indices for a 76 GB corpus need 188 GB, too large for personal devices, so a smaller index is needed.

sections.body: Vector search returns the top-k vectors nearest a query. Approximate search is used because exact search needs a linear scan, and recall is the fraction of true top-k neighbors returned. The section compares two index types. IVF groups vectors into clusters and is cheaper to build, with less index structure. Proximity graphs connect similar vectors and answer queries by best-first traversal, needing far fewer distance computations. In that search, the parameter ef bounds the candidate queue, and a larger ef raises recall at the cost of more distance computations. The section states that graph search needs about O(log N) embedding extractions and distance computations per query.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Proximity graph indices need few distance computations, but storage has two parts: vectors and index metadata.

sections.body: Offline, LEANN computes embeddings, builds a graph, prunes it to keep high-degree nodes, discards dense embeddings, and stores a PQ table. If a peak storage budget is set, it builds and merges shards in sequence. Online, a two-level search uses PQ distances to pick candidates, then recomputes exact embeddings for the most promising ones in batches. The pruned graph stores integer entries in proportion to node count and average degree, and the PQ codebook is 100 times smaller than the FP32 embeddings. The section says the design targets user devices and may suit data lakes with cold datasets, where infrequent queries make recomputation inexpensive.
sections.heading: LEANN Overview
sections.headline: LEANN keeps a pruned graph and product-quantized codes, recomputing exact embeddings during queries.

sections.body: Approximate PQ distances guide exploration, and exact distances are computed only for the top alpha percent of candidates not yet in the exact queue. Selected candidates are recomputed exactly and inserted into that queue, so traversal keeps exact-distance quality. The authors state that re-ranking more approximate neighbors would not help when ground-truth neighbors are missed during traversal. Dynamic batching groups candidates across several exploration steps until a target batch size is reached, such as 64, chosen by offline profiling. The section states a trade-off: batching introduces slight staleness in the exploration order in exchange for higher GPU utilization than single-step processing.
sections.heading: Graph-based Recomputation
sections.headline: Two-level search and dynamic batching cut recomputation while keeping exact distances for selected candidates.

sections.body: The formulation minimizes recomputations per exploration step under a storage budget and a recall threshold, with each stored neighbor ID taking 4 bytes. Random edge removal and a lower degree limit both reduce accuracy even under mild size reductions, because graph connectivity suffers. The method lets the top 2% of nodes by degree keep up to M connections, while other nodes are capped at a lower limit m, set to one fifth of M. M is chosen by offline profiling for a given budget. Nodes also link bidirectionally to newly inserted nodes up to M, so ordinary nodes can still reach hubs. The method uses node degree as a proxy for node importance, which the section takes as an assumption.
sections.heading: Compact Graph Structure
sections.headline: Preserving edges of the top 2% high-degree nodes shrinks graph metadata while maintaining high retrieval accuracy.

sections.body: LEANN builds the index in three stages under a storage limit. First, k-means on a subset yields k centroids, and each object is assigned to its two nearest centroids, with embeddings discarded after assignment. Second, each shard graph is built with embeddings recomputed and then discarded, and the two-centroid overlap gives global connectivity. Third, shard graphs are merged: shared nodes take the higher HNSW level, and lower-level edge lists are merged with random edge drops above degree M. The authors call the result well connected and leave RNG-based pruning to future work. For updates, deletions mark nodes inactive, and batched additions are buffered and inserted asynchronously after a search.
sections.heading: Index Building and Update
sections.headline: Sharded construction and buffered updates limit peak storage during index building and modification.

sections.body: Experiments use RPJ-Wiki, about 76 GB of text split into 60 million passages, which yields about 173 GB of Contriever embeddings. Tests run on an RTX 4090 with 32 GB RAM, on four QA datasets and three personal datasets. Only LEANN and IVF-Recompute stay below 5% of the 76 GB raw dataset. HNSW stores full embeddings with graph padding, DiskANN reaches 270 GB, and PQ needs an extra 15 GB of graph metadata. Latency is measured at 90% recall. LEANN standalone search is slower than HNSW and DiskANN, but it adds less than 20% overhead to end-to-end RAG. IVF-Recompute is up to 200 times slower than LEANN, and BM25 and PQ fail to reach 90% recall.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: LEANN matches the accuracy of the standard graph index at 90% recall while storing about 5% of raw data size.

sections.body: Disk-based systems such as DiskANN, Starling and FusionANNS keep compressed embeddings in memory or move them to disk, and AiSAQ and LM-DiskANN also keep compressed embeddings on disk. EdgeRAG generates embeddings online through an IVF index but still has high storage and recomputation overhead. MicroNN and ObjectBox target personal devices yet store all embeddings. Product quantization and RabitQ save space but lose accuracy under tight budgets. The section positions LEANN as combining on-the-fly recomputation with a pruned graph and optimized traversal for personal devices. It also cites on-device RAG and personalized recommendation as applications that need low-overhead search on personal devices.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier systems reduce memory via disk layouts, quantization or online embedding but still store embeddings.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the design. Two-level search with dynamic batching allows queries without storing the full embedding set, and high-degree preserving pruning reduces graph storage while maintaining accuracy. The construction and update pipelines are also storage-efficient. The section reports an index smaller than 5% of raw data size, up to 50 times storage reduction compared with existing methods, while preserving high recall and low latency. It frames the work as supporting generative AI applications such as RAG, where embedding and index storage is the obstacle. The conclusion adds no measurements beyond those in the earlier sections.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: LEANN keeps the index under 5% of raw data size, up to 50 times smaller than existing methods, with high recall.

sections.body: Appendix A defines RNG pruning, which drops a candidate x when a closer neighbor a gives Dist(a,x) less than Dist(v,x), and notes that it makes the graph very sparse. Appendix B gives the add operation's complexity, which falls from O(M efC + efC^2 + M^3) to O(M efC) through a distance cache and simplified pruning, and describes soft deletion and delayed batched insertion. Table 4 reports Mac latency under the same protocol, where HNSW and IVF run out of memory. Appendix D reports that 15 shards cut peak construction storage about 5 times, that GTE-small gives a 2.3 times speedup within 2% of Contriever accuracy, and that caching 10% of embeddings gives a 1.5 times speedup. Embedding recomputation accounts for roughly 76% of latency.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers relative neighborhood graph pruning, update algorithms, Mac latency, and ablations on construction, embedding model, caching, and latency breakdown.
